title: AI document processing: how accurate is it on financial documents?
description: We benchmarked AI tools on 30 fund reports, with answers locked in advance. Which ones made no mistakes, what each costs per report, and how to set it up.
summary: Document AI reads a PDF or scan and returns the fields your systems use, like totals and dates[^3][^4]. OCR returns raw text only; document AI knows which number is which[^2][^3]. Start with the document your team re-keys most: reading costs cents, and staff time is the real cost[^5][^1].
verdict: Have two models from different vendors read each file; a person settles their disagreements[^9][^10].
AI reading costs cents per report; staff time and errors are the real cost[^5][^1].
The two best models made zero mistakes on our 30 fund reports[^5].
Thirty clean reports still allow a true error rate of up to about 1 in 10[^13].
First step: benchmark two models on 50 files from one team's queue[^14].

pickElse: Thousands of standard invoices a day? A prebuilt cloud parser, a ready-made reader for standard forms, costs about a penny a page[^2][^4].

Your files cannot leave your network: run an open-source model on your own servers. Expect more wrong values: in our first round the two local models made 8 each, where Anthropic's Claude Haiku 5.5 made none[^5].
You only need searchable text, not fields: basic text recognition (OCR) costs well under a penny a page at all three big clouds[^2][^3][^4].

ownData.title: Which AI made the fewest mistakes on 30 fund reports?
ownData.intro: FinExtractBench is our own benchmark of 30 public private-fund reports, 781 pages in all[^5]. We wrote every right answer by hand and locked it before any tool ran[^5]. Each tool read each raw PDF once; a mistake is a wrong value or a value the report never states.
rows: Gemini 4 Carbon (Google; a weaker model, for comparison)
ownData.note: Limits: one person wrote the answers, and the reports are digital, in English and 56 pages at most[^5]. Zero mistakes in 30 reports still allows a true rate of up to about 1 report in 10[^13]. Re-run on 10 reports as scanned page images, both tools still made 0 mistakes[^5].

example.input: A 57-page quarterly report from a private equity fund, as a PDF.
example.output: Money committed (commitment), money paid in (paid-in capital), money paid back out (distributions), and what the fund is worth today (NAV, net asset value). Each fact comes with its page number and the exact words it came from. Any fact the two models disagree on is flagged.

howToTest: Record today's baseline first: staff minutes per file, and errors that reach the systems and reports downstream.
Pick 50 real files, including your worst scans and longest reports, plus facts some files never state, to catch invented answers. Even vendors advise benchmarking on your own documents[^14].
Write the right answer for every fact before any AI reads the files, and lock it, so the AI's output cannot sway it.
Require each answer to name its page and quote the exact words, and have code check that the quote is there.
Count wrong answers apart from blanks. A blank goes to a person; a wrong number can slip through.
Report minutes per file, wrong fields reaching downstream systems and cost per file, before and after. Run the winner again on new files before you go live.

buyVsBuild.buy: Buy a prebuilt parser or an accounts payable tool when your files are standard invoices, receipts or IDs. The big clouds' prebuilt models already cover those[^2][^4]. Buying fits best when you mainly need volume and an audit trail.
buyVsBuild.build: Build on frontier models (the newest, most capable ones) when your files are unique to your business and a wrong number is expensive. The build is a prompt, a fact list, a checker and a review queue where your team settles about 2 facts per report[^5]. If files must stay in-house, run an open-source model on your own servers; in our benchmark, local models made more wrong values[^5].

watchOuts: Vendor accuracy numbers mostly come from the vendor's own benchmark runs[^14], and public answer keys have errors too[^12]. Even on our locked-answer set, when the AI and our key differed, the AI was right in 22 of 57 cases, so check your key[^5].
A model that writes a plausible wrong number is worse than one that leaves the field blank[^11]. Score them separately.
Two tables on one page with similar labels fooled 7 of 10 tools in our hard round[^5]. Check the facts that sit near look-alikes.
Prices and model versions change: Mistral's newer OCR model costs twice its older one[^6]. Re-run your benchmark when either changes, and keep the files and answers so the re-run is cheap.
Read the vendor's data terms. Datalab's rate card shows prices with a 25% discount that assumes you let it train on your data[^7].
Plan reviewer time: in our benchmark, about 1 fact in 4 (66 of 270) went to a person[^5]. Multiply by the facts you pull each month to size the workload.

sources.name: Xiong et al., Can LLMs Express Their Uncertainty? (2023)
sources.what: Finds that language models tend to be overconfident when they state their own confidence.

sources.name: Cohen et al., LM vs LM (EMNLP 2023)
sources.what: Having a second model question the first catches factual errors better than earlier methods, often by a large gap.

sources.name: Manakul et al., SelfCheckGPT (EMNLP 2023)
sources.what: Facts that disagree across several answers to the same question are likely invented; consistent facts are likely true.

sources.name: OpenAI, Why language models hallucinate (2025)
sources.what: Argues errors are worse than abstentions and evaluations should penalise confident errors more than uncertainty.

sources.name: Northcutt et al., Pervasive label errors in test sets (2021)
sources.what: Finds at least 3.3% wrong answers on average across 10 widely used benchmark answer keys.

sources.name: Newman, JAMA 1995, interpreting small numerators
sources.what: With zero events in N trials, the upper 95% confidence limit for the true rate is about 3/N.

sources.name: Mistral, OCR 4 announcement
sources.what: Mistral ran most of its OCR 4 comparisons itself and advises users to evaluate on their own documents.

sources.name: EU AI Act, Annex III
sources.what: Lists credit scoring of people and life and health insurance pricing as high-risk uses.

sources.name: EU AI Act, Article 12
sources.what: High-risk AI systems must automatically record events (logs) over their lifetime.

sources.name: EU AI Act, Article 14
sources.what: High-risk AI systems must be designed so that people can oversee them effectively.

sources.name: Council of the EU, AI omnibus final approval (30 Jun 2026)
sources.what: Rules for stand-alone high-risk AI systems now apply from 2 December 2027.

sources.name: Lewis Silkin, Digital Omnibus on AI in force (Jul 2026)
sources.what: The omnibus defers Annex III high-risk obligations to 2 December 2027.

sources.name: 12 CFR 1002.9 (Cornell LII)
sources.what: Adverse action notices must give specific principal reasons; citing a failed score alone is not enough.

sources.name: CFPB Circular 2022-03
sources.what: Creditors using complex algorithms must still disclose the specific principal reasons for a denial.

sources.name: NYDFS Circular Letter No. 7 (2024)
sources.what: Insurers stay responsible for vendor AI tools in underwriting and pricing and should seek audit rights in vendor contracts.

rules.name: EU AI Act, Annex III
rules.what: Reading documents is not a high-risk use on its own. It becomes part of one when the facts feed credit scoring of people or life and health insurance pricing[^15]. Then logging and human oversight apply[^16][^17], from 2 December 2027[^18][^19].

rules.name: Regulation B, 12 CFR 1002.9
rules.what: If extracted facts feed a US credit decision, a decline still needs specific reasons[^20], even when an algorithm made it[^21]. A wrongly read fact becomes a wrong reason, so keep the page and quote behind every fact.

rules.name: NYDFS Circular Letter No. 7
rules.what: New York insurers that use AI in underwriting and pricing stay responsible for vendor tools[^22]. Where available, their vendor contracts should give them audit rights[^22].
